h1: Third Stage of Labor Anatomy: Placental Delivery and Hemostasis
blurb: After the baby is born, interlacing uterine muscle fibers contract like living ligatures to constrict spiral arteries and cleanly deliver the placenta.
lead: Minutes after birth, figure-of-eight muscle fibers in the uterine wall clamp down around spiral arteries like living ligatures as the placenta cleanly separates. In this illustrated guide to third stage of labor anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including infant birth, placenta before separation, uterine myometrium, uterine retraction—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Minutes after birth, figure-of-eight muscle fibers in the uterine wall clamp down around spiral arteries like living ligatures as the placenta cleanly separates. The third stage begins immediately after the baby is born and ends when placenta and membranes are delivered. Uterine contraction reduces the attachment area and compresses maternal vessels to limit bleeding. The NEW post-birth teaching cutaway depicts a partially detaching placenta with an empty uterus; it is NOT a patient image or a photograph of a completely delivered placenta. A second older image separately shows the organ still attached during pregnancy and a third digital image depicts its villous exchange barrier BEFORE delivery. Clinicians assess completion and bleeding in real patients; heavy bleeding after birth is an emergency. questions.question: When does the third stage of labor begin and end?
questions.answer: It begins after the baby is born and ends when the placenta and fetal membranes are delivered. Postpartum monitoring continues after that stage. Structurally, the end of third stage comprises after placenta and membranes are delivered, third stage ends and postpartum recovery follows. Physiologically, the end of third stage governs marks transition to postnatal assessment.

questions.question: Why does the uterus contract after the baby is born?
questions.answer: Uterine contraction shrinks the placental attachment area, supports separation and compresses maternal blood vessels to limit bleeding. Actual uterine tone must be assessed clinically. Structurally, the uterine tone comprises postpartum uterine contraction compresses placental-bed vessels. Physiologically, the uterine tone governs limits bleeding after placental separation.

questions.question: Which surfaces does a delivered placenta have?
questions.answer: A fetal-facing surface is covered by amnion and joined to the cord, while a maternal-facing surface reflects its attachment to uterine decidual tissue. Examination of a delivered placenta is a clinical task. Structurally, the maternal placental surface comprises decidual-facing surface includes separated maternal tissue and placental lobules. Physiologically, the maternal placental surface forms former uterine attachment interface.
